https://www.rferl.org/a/us-congressman-a.body: Armenia US Congressman Abraham Hamadeh: Armenia-Azerbaijan Peace Deal Could Come Before Trump's Term Ends By Alex Raufoglu September 10, 2026 13:46 CET US Congressman Abraham Hamadeh: Armenia-Azerbaijan Peace Deal Could Come Before Trump's Term Ends Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinian (right) welcomes US Congressman Abraham Hamadeh in Yerevan in August. WASHINGTON -- US Congressman Abraham Hamadeh says the Armenia-Azerbaijan peace process is moving faster than many expected and predicts a final peace agreement could be reached well before the end of President Donald Trump's current term. Hamadeh, a Republican from Arizona and a member of the House Armed Services and Veterans' Affairs committees, has emerged as an active congressional interlocutor on the South Caucasus. He visited Azerbaijan in June and Armenia in August and met with the countries' leaders. In an interview with RFE/RL on September 9, Hamadeh described the proposed Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP) as more than an economic project, arguing it could bind Armenia and Azerbaijan together politically and economically while opening the South Caucasus to greater Western trade and investment. Unveiled as part of the US-mediated peace process following Armenia's war with Azerbaijan over its breakaway region of Nagorno-Karabakh, TRIPP envisages rail and road infrastructure, possible oil and gas pipelines, and fiberoptic and electricity ventures. Armenia and Azerbaijan fought for more than three decades over Nagorno-Karabakh, an Azerbaijani region populated mainly by ethnic Armenians. Normalization gained momentum after Azerbaijan retook the territory in 2023 and a Washington peace summit in August 2025 helped break the deadlock. RFE/RL: You recently visited Azerbaijan and Armenia and met with the leaders of both countries. What obstacles still stand in the way of turning a peace declaration into a final and lasting peace? Abraham Hamadeh: We should look at where we were just one year ago. One year ago, in August, was when you had both [Armenian Prime Minister Nikol] Pashinian and [Azerbaijani President Ilham] Aliyev here at the White House with Trump, something that nobody ever saw coming, especially this quickly, where you had this agreement for peace, and now we are off to the races. I bet you know Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio have been so instrumental, and even Vice President JD Vance has been to the region. It looks like US government officials at all levels are committed to this. My involvement with this was meeting with the Armenian ambassador and Azerbaijani ambassador separately, and getting them together. They both came to Arizona at my brother's house. They've both been to an event for me in Mar-a-Lago. We have a great relationship, so we're trying to make sure and ensure that this peace is solidified. Any of the obstacles are, to be honest, just time. It takes time for emotions to settle down after being in a period of war and for decades of war. And so, from my experience being over there, both in Baku and Yerevan, it's going very smoothly, and both sides are absolutely committed to ensuring the South Caucasus is peaceful and prosperous. US Congressman Abraham Hamadeh RFE/RL: The next challenge is implementation. What should peace look like on the ground in terms of borders, transport, trade, prisoners, security? Hamadeh: Yes, there's still some challenges, of course. There are some prisoners the Armenians would like back from Azerbaijan. Each side has their own opinions on all of these issues. One of the things I believe is going to help is not just Azerbaijan and Armenia's relationship, but Turkey and Armenia's relationship, which I think has been a little bit understated lately. Both sides agreed to open up their borders to start off with diplomatic crossings back in 2022. That still has not been implemented yet. We hope to see their border open up just so that Armenia gets another avenue for trade other than going to Russia or Georgia or Iran. So we need to ensure the Turkish border with Armenia opens up. We need to make sure the Azerbaijan and Armenia TRIPP goes well. But all this -- again, it's been only one year, and in terms of history, it's so new. So everything is going well, and both leaders are very popular within their countries, and they have to support the people, which is very important. TRIPP: Much More Than Just Economics RFE/RL: You describe TRIPP as central to the future of the region. Do you see the proposed corridor primarily as an economic project, or as something that could itself help guarantee and sustain regional peace? And if TRIPP were delayed or politically blocked, could that put the peace process at risk? Hamadeh: I see no reason why it's going to be delayed. TRIPP is much more than just economics. Of course, it's going to benefit the economies of both countries, but it's going to solidify them and tie them so much diplomatically, politically, economically. Map: Proposed Trump Route For International Peace And Prosperity (TRIPP) They are neighbors, and there's a long history between the two. It's going to take time for it to happen, but I am so confident with this TRIPP corridor -- named after Trump, of course -- that once the construction begins, once it's fully operational, the amount of opportunity for the South Caucasus is immense. The reason people don't talk about the South Caucasus much is because a lot of people don't even know where that is on a map. But I recognize, having been there and having been a student of history there, the Russians are becoming less influential in the South Caucasus, which is a big benefit for the US. The Iranians are totally decimated; they're distracted right now. So the Caucasus of Georgia, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Turkey's help -- they have a lot of potential to be that bridge between Asia, especially Central Asia, which is also very understated, connecting them to the Caucasus, through the Caspian Sea, through this TRIPP corridor to beyond, to Turkey, into Europe. Right now Azerbaijan provides so much gas to Europe. Sixteen to seventeen countries are exporting this gas. They provide 25 percent of Italy's natural gas. I mean, it's remarkable. So there's already so much development happening now. Just imagine when this TRIPP corridor is actually fully operational. RFE/RL: Moscow has increasingly criticized the proposed "Trump route," most recently with Russian Security Council Deputy Secretary Aleksei Shevtsov suggesting its implementation could allow the US to deploy troops or intelligence capabilities in Armenia. What is your response to those claims? Hamadeh: This has nothing to do with a US military presence. We've got plenty of presence in the Middle East and in Turkey, but this is a peace between two countries that's been long overdue. This is classic Russian disinformation. They're trying to destabilize Armenia, which is a democracy; it's one of the most stable democracies in the region. So they are trying to just discredit Pashinian right now with some of the population. The Russian influence with Armenia is stronger than, say, in the other Caucasus countries, and you can't trust the Russians. And right now they're very much distracted by the Ukrainian war...and they're realizing there's this big void that the United States is stepping into right now. We are the ones making peace possible. The Russians have had their influence in those countries, and they've disappointed both of them. https://www.rferl.org/a/russia-migrant-w.body: Russia 'Organized Slavery': Russia's Tighter Migrant Rules Could Hit Central Asian Workers, Worsen Shortages By Azattyq Asia August 16, 2026 14:34 CET Listen 7 min This audio is automated Learn more 'Organized Slavery': Russia's Tighter Migrant Rules Could Hit Central Asian Workers, Worsen Shortages Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google About 3 million foreigners were working in Russia at the beginning of 2026, many of them from Central Asian countries. (file photo) Russia is proposing an overhaul of its system for recruiting foreign workers beginning in 2027, tying migrants to specific employers, jobs, and regions in a move authorities say will give the state greater control over labor migration. But the plan is already drawing concern from migration experts and businesses. They warn that tighter restrictions could drive migrant workers into informal employment and further worsen workforce shortages in a country that relies heavily on foreign labor. The four-year experiment, scheduled to run from January 1, 2027, through the end of 2030, would cover 87 Russian regions, excluding Moscow and the Moscow region. Russian authorities estimate that more than 1.7 million foreign workers could be affected, including large numbers from Central Asia. The new system would move away from the “work-patent” mechanism that has been the main route to legal employment for migrants from visa-free countries such as Uzbekistan and Tajikistan. In 2025, foreigners obtained about 2.3 million Russian work patents, according to Interior Ministry figures. That represented more than 40 percent of all foreigners in Russia and almost 77 percent of officially employed foreign workers. SEE ALSO: Central Asian Schoolchildren Caught Up In Russia's Crackdown On Migrants Russia remains heavily dependent on foreign labor. About 3 million foreigners were officially working in the country at the beginning of 2026, while the total number of foreign nationals in Russia, including migrants’ family members, exceeded 5.7 million, according to the ministry. Under the proposed system, migrants would arrive in Russia already matched with a particular employer and vacancy. A new information system would maintain registries of employers and foreign workers and match workers with jobs based on regional labor-market needs. The system would also expand the amount of information authorities collect on migrants before they enter Russia. In addition to photographs and fingerprints, migrants would undergo mandatory genomic registration and medical examinations. 'No Rights For The Migrant' For migrants, however, the biggest change could be the loss of freedom to change jobs. Under the proposed rules, once in Russia, workers recruited through the new system would not be allowed to work for a different employer, in a different profession, or outside the region specified in the registry until their employment contracts expire. SEE ALSO: Russia's Migrant Crackdown Expands With Mandatory Mobile Tracking Violating those rules could result in removal from the foreign-worker registry and an obligation to leave Russia. Such workers could then only reenter the system and regain the ability to work in Russia after a year. “During my nearly 15 years in Russia, I have always stayed in the same city, but I changed my work several times with different private construction companies, depending on the money and conditions they offered,” Sarvar, a Tajik worker in the Russian city of Surgut, told RFE/RL. “I don’t know much about this plan yet, but I fear that if my employer knows that I can’t easily change my job, it would be difficult for me to negotiate my salary or other things.” A Russian traffic policeman checks the documents of guest workers from Central Asia. (file photo) Valentina Chupik, a human-rights advocate who heads Tong Jahoni, an organization that assists migrants, said the restrictions could leave workers particularly vulnerable to abusive employers. “There will be no rights for the migrant. He will be firmly attached to the employer,” Chupik said, describing the proposed system as “organized slavery.” The government says the new model is intended to make migration more transparent and reduce illegal employment by giving authorities more information about workers before they arrive. It also says the model is intended to increase employers’ responsibilities. Divided Opinion The proposed changes have divided migration experts. Mikhail Burda, head of the Center for Migration Studies at the Moscow-based Tsargrad Institute, argues that the country will remain attractive because of the size of its labor market and its established ties with Central Asia. “Targeted organized recruitment should become the only possible procedure for temporary employment in Russia for mass migration,” Burda said. “The formula ‘come, work, leave’ should be implemented in its absolute sense, without reservations or exceptions.” SEE ALSO: Thousands Of Central Asians Enlisted To Fight Russia's War In Ukraine Through 'Coercion, Enticements' Karimjon Yorov, a Tajik migration expert, takes a sharply different view. He said the additional procedures and restrictions could make it harder for Central Asian workers to enter Russia. “I can say with confidence that there is nothing good in it,” Yorov said. “Unfortunately, the consequences will be bad...for all migrants.” Yorov warned that the new recruitment system could create opportunities for corruption if intermediaries begin charging migrants for access to jobs or recruitment lists. He recalled that when work permits cost 1,000 to 2,000 rubles ($12-$24 at current exchange rates), they were sometimes resold for 20,000 to 50,000 rubles ($240-$600). Russia’s business community is also worried about the potential consequences. The Russian Union of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs has warned the government that tying migrants to a single employer could push some workers out of the formal economy. The group wants migrants to be allowed to work for multiple employers and for the process of changing jobs to be made easier. The business group has also proposed delaying the experiment from 2027 to 2028 and introducing a two-year transition period during which the new system would operate alongside existing patent and work-permit mechanisms. Moscow has begun reviewing its agreements with Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, two major sources of migrant labor, on organized recruitment. Yorov told RFE/RL that Tajikistan has begun preparing for the new system, with centers being established to prepare prospective migrants and conduct medical examinations, fingerprinting, and photography. Written by Farangis Najibullah based on reporting by Azattyq Asia. https://www.rferl.org/a/russian-minors-a.body: Russia Hundreds Of Russian Teens Face Terrorism Charges As Wartime Crackdown Intensifies By RFE/RL's Russian Service and Current Time September 08, 2026 22:08 CET Listen 6 min This audio is automated Learn more Hundreds Of Russian Teens Face Terrorism Charges As Wartime Crackdown Intensifies Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Russian police officers push a teenager during a protest rally in St. Petersburg. (file photo) Vitalina Prening, a 16-year-old Russian schoolgirl, was recently charged with planning a terrorist attack, membership in a terrorist organization, and undergoing terrorist training, according to Russian media. From the city of Novosibirsk, Prening was added to Russia's terrorist blacklist on August 10, although details of the charges against her remain unclear. On social media, those who know Prening have portrayed her as an accomplished youth who drew, sang, practiced ballroom dancing, and participated in state-sponsored public events. Prening is not alone. Hundreds of Russian teenagers have been charged with terrorism, sabotage, extremism, or treason since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Human rights campaigners say the arrest and jailing of teenagers is part of an intensifying campaign to stifle dissent during wartime. 'Greater Repressive Activity' Department One, an exiled legal and human rights organization that defends Russians accused of treason and espionage, said in a July report that at least 779 minors are on Russia's terrorist and extremist registry. Nearly 97 percent of them were added after 2022. The list includes not only those who have been convicted of crimes but also people formally named as suspects or facing active charges. The banned human rights group Memorial said at least 124 minors are currently facing criminal charges in Russia for political reasons. Rights groups say an increasing number of minors are being prosecuted under controversial terrorism and extremism laws, with trials frequently held behind closed doors. SEE ALSO: Russian Children Reportedly Beaten, Injured At Patriotic Camp Funded By Kremlin The cases range from anti-war activism and online criticism of the authorities to allegations that the teenagers were recruited by Ukrainian intelligence services through social media to carry out acts of sabotage and terrorism on Russian soil. Sergei Davidis, head of Memorial's political prisoner support project, told RFE/RL that the war has intensified political repression in Russia. "The state exhibits far greater repressive activity in a war situation," Davidis said. Arrested For Distributing Leaflets Among the minors who have been caught up in the crackdown is Arseny Turbin, who was 15 when he was arrested in 2023. Turbin had distributed leaflets criticizing President Vladimir Putin, created a Telegram channel called Free Russia, and photographed himself with a white-blue-white flag used by Russian anti-war protesters. SEE ALSO: One Of Russia's Youngest Political Prisoners Turns 18. And He Faces New Charges. His mother, Irina Turbina, said her son openly told investigators that he believed Russia was the aggressor in the war. In 2024, a Russian court sentenced Turbin to five years in prison during a closed trial. Two years later, the authorities opened another case against the teenager, accusing him of participating in unrest at his penal colony. The youngest teenager currently on Russia's terrorist and extremist registry is believed to be Ivan Maltsev, 14, who was accused of attempting to set fire to a police car. His father has denied the charges against his son. Maltsev, a resident of the Siberian city of Barnaul, turned 14 in June, the minimum age of criminal responsibility in Russia for serious crimes, including terrorism. 'Atmosphere Of Fear' Rights campaigners have accused Russian security agencies of using provocative tactics against minors. "They push young people to create some kind of group, write some harsh statements, provoke them, for example, they write something in the comments so that you are practically compelled to respond," Dmitry Zair-Bek, head of Department One, told RFE/RL. Embed share Buzz Builds For Russian Singer Sentenced To More Time by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:01:37 0:00 Security officials, Zair-Bek said, would then "lead" vulnerable young people to committing an act that could be formally defined as a crime, allowing operatives to open a criminal case against them. "What's monstrous is that children and teenagers are being persecuted for things they shouldn't be persecuted for at all," Zair-Bek said, citing "careless jokes" on social media, messages in school forums, and discussions in computer games. Olga Romanova, head of the civil rights group Russia Behind Bars, told RFE/RL that the secrecy surrounding terrorism cases allows Russian security agencies to increase their conviction rates. "Terrorism cases -- the investigations and trials are completely closed," Romanova said. "It's supposedly classified information, so there's no need to prove anything." Zair-Bek said the growing number of cases also serves a broader purpose: creating a climate of fear. "The whole atmosphere of fear that is created, including through the mass initiation of terrorism and extremism cases, is connected to the fact that repression works in our time, in the 21st century, only when it is constantly increasing," he said. https://www.rferl.org/a/china-xinjiang-k.body: China China's New 'Ethnic Unity' Law Looms Over Closed-Door Trial Of Kazakh Writer By Zamira Eshanova August 14, 2026 12:41 CET China's New 'Ethnic Unity' Law Looms Over Closed-Door Trial Of Kazakh Writer Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Zhengis Reskhan (left) with members of his family in an undated handout photo. After months of uncertainty, the family of prominent ethnic Kazakh writer and satirist Zhengis Reskhan has learned that he faces a closed-door trial in China and could spend a decade in prison. Reskhan has been detained since March 19 following months of police interrogations. Until now, his family had received no official confirmation of where he was being held and had no contact with him. Reskhan’s family says Chinese police had previously accused him of having “extremist” ideas, an allegation conveyed to them verbally. He is now accused of “undermining ethnic unity,” according to his son, Nartai Zhengis. Nartai said his father’s trial is scheduled for August 15 and will be held in secret. He told RFE/RL’s Kazakh Service that his father’s lawyer informed the family that “no one will be allowed to attend the trial.” Reskhan’s wife, Nartai’s mother, will also be barred from the proceedings, he said, adding that the lawyer told him that once the court issues its verdict “the only information that might be made public would be something like: ‘He was sentenced to this many years in prison.’” SEE ALSO: Family Seeks Answers After Prominent Kazakh Writer Disappears In Xinjiang The family has been told that Reskhan could face up to 10 years’ imprisonment if convicted. Nartai said the “undermining ethnic unity” allegation had been added to the earlier accusation that his father was guilty of “extremist thought.” The family has not seen an indictment or other court documents identifying the legal basis for the accusation. A Test Case? The charge comes shortly after China’s Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress took effect on July 1. Adopted by the National People’s Congress in March, the controversial measure establishes a broad legal framework for interethnic relations and includes provisions concerning conduct deemed to undermine ethnic unity. Whether the allegation against Reskhan is being brought under the new law remains unclear. If the case falls under this legislation, it could provide an early indication of how the law is being applied to ethnic minority defendants. SEE ALSO: Fears Mount In Kazakhstan As Beijing's 'Ethnic Unity Law' Looms Across The Border Beijing says its provisions will “strengthen the rule of law” and "better protect” the rights of China's 56 officially recognized ethnic groups. The measure, however, has drawn criticism from advocacy organizations, UN experts, the European Union, and Western governments over concerns that it could further restrict minority rights and extend Beijing's ethnic policies beyond China's borders. UN experts warned in April that the statute risked entrenching “a uniform approach to ethnic relations across all regions,” while Human Rights Watch and the European Parliament have called for its repeal. Beijing has rejected international criticism of the legislation as a “malicious smear” and interference in China's internal affairs. Separately, Amnesty International issued a call on July 14 calling for Reskhan's immediate release unless Chinese authorities can provide “sufficient credible and admissible evidence” that he committed an internationally recognized criminal offense. ' Unlawful From The Very Beginning' Chinese authorities have remained tight-lipped about Reskhan’s case, including the legal basis for the allegations against him. “We have received no response whatsoever from the Chinese side,” his son said. As a Kazakh citizen living in Kazakhstan, Nartai has appealed to Astana to intervene -- a sensitive issue for a government that has long balanced concerns over the treatment of ethnic Kazakhs in China with close political and economic ties to Beijing. According to Nartai, the Kazakh Foreign Ministry told him that his father is a Chinese citizen and that the case falls under Beijing’s jurisdiction. The ministry advised the family to seek assistance from the relevant Chinese authorities, he said. SEE ALSO: Court In Kazakhstan Finds All 19 Defendants Guilty For Anti-China Protests While Astana has declined to intervene, Nartai has rejected the allegations against his father and said the proceedings have no legal basis. “Everything that my father is currently going through and experiencing, whether under international law or under the laws of the People’s Republic of China itself, is unlawful from the very beginning up to the present day,” he said. “It violates China’s own laws as well as every applicable legal standard.” Nartai also accused officials in Xinjiang of targeting his father because of his professional achievements and reputation. “This is the work of people within the local government in Xinjiang, China, people who blindly carry out orders, who are envious of and unable to accept my father’s achievements and successes in his position, as well as the respect and standing he has earned within the country,” he said. A writer and satirist from Xinjiang, Reskhan has worked as a teacher, editor, and cultural official. He is a member of the China Writers Association and the Xinjiang Writers Association and previously served as chairman of the Hami Regional Writers Association. He has published 13 literary works, mainly children’s literature and humorous writing, several of which have been officially translated from Kazakh into Chinese. SEE ALSO: Uyghur Camp Survivor Details Forced Sterilization, Torture In Xinjiang Reskhan's case comes against the backdrop of years of repression in Xinjiang, where ethnic Kazakhs, Uyghurs, and other predominantly Muslim minorities have faced mass detention and restrictions on their cultural, religious, and linguistic rights. Beijing maintains its policies in Xinjiang are aimed at combating terrorism and extremism and denies allegations of widespread abuses. Rights groups, former detainees, and Western governments, however, have rejected those claims, while a 2022 UN human rights assessment said allegations of arbitrary detention and other abuses in Xinjiang were credible and could constitute crimes against humanity. https://www.rferl.org/a/bishkek-kyrgyz-s.body: News Amid Setbacks, Putin Looks To Restore Russia's Standing At Bishkek SCO Summit By RFE/RL August 31, 2026 00:43 CET Listen 6 min This audio is automated Learn more Amid Setbacks, Putin Looks To Restore Russia's Standing At Bishkek SCO Summit Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Russian President Vladimir Putin (right) and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi shake hands during a meeting on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Bishkek on August 31. Facing increasing confrontations with the West, Russian President Vladimir Putin is looking eastward to restore his country's standing in the region at a major summit in Bishkek, the Kyrgyz capital. It comes at a time of increased difficulties for the Kremlin leader, with Russia's economy in tatters due to Western sanctions and Ukrainian drone strikes, ally Iran battered in war, and the leaders of former client states such as Syria and Venezuela ousted amid a muted Moscow response. Putin is set to hold bilateral meetings with at least nine world leaders, including Iranian President Masud Pezeshkian, starting on August 31 on the sidelines of the two-day Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO), which is celebrating its 25th anniversary. SEE ALSO: Aggressive Recruiters Are Rounding Up Russians To Fight In Ukraine. In One Town, They're Pushing Back On the first day, the Russian leader met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Putin and Xi focused on bilateral issues and only discussed the war in Ukraine "marginally...essentially there was no discussion." Western nations have called on China to use its influence to pressure the Kremlin into ending its war on Ukraine. Russia's Interfax news agency reported Modi told Putin that India supported "every peace effort" to end the war in Ukraine, without providing further details. Putin is also expected to hold bilateral sessions with leaders of non-SCO nations, including Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinian, who has angered the Kremlin by seeking closer ties to the West for his small Caucasus nation. United Front Putin and Xi have often used SCO gatherings to put up a united front against Western influence in the region. Xi arrived late on August 30 and held his first meeting with Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov, who will serve as host of the summit. Along with Russia, Iran, India, and China, the SCO grouping consists of Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, Uzbekistan, and Tajikistan. Not all members are allies, of course, with nuclear powers Pakistan and India often on the brink of war with each other. Russian President Vladimir Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi greet each other on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in Bishkek on August 31. The organization began as the "Shanghai Five" in 1996 but began expanding to other regional nations starting in 2001. Moscow and Tehran are both under crippling Western sanctions -- Russia for its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and Iran for a multitude of issues, including its support for extremist activity in the Middle East and its alleged pursuit of a nuclear weapon. Kyiv and the West have demanded Iran cease from providing deadly Shahed drones to Russia for use in the Ukraine war, while US officials told RFE/RL that Russia is providing Iran with targeting information to attack US troops and military assets in the Middle East, confirming a Washington Post report . 'Key Subjects' Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov said "one of the key subjects" in the talks between Putin and Pezeshkian will be the Middle East crisis. "You know how relevant this meeting is in light of the current uneasy atmosphere in the Middle East and the situation surrounding Iran," he added. Also on the agenda will be the $25 billion agreement signed by Tehran with Russia's state nuclear company Rosatom to build four nuclear power plants in Iran. Leaders of SCO nations attend the 2025 summit in the Chinese city of Tianjin. Naser al-Tamimi, a UK-based analyst and founder of MidEast Strategia, wrote on X that the SCO can help largely isolated Iran, "but only to a point." "The SCO offers Iran broader political cover, helps reduce its international isolation, and expands opportunities for trade and settlements in yuan, rubles, and other national currencies. In doing so, it can modestly reduce Tehran's dependence on the Western financial system." "But the SCO is not an economic shield against US sanctions. It lacks a fully developed alternative financial architecture, provides no reliable protection for major banks and companies exposed to secondary sanctions, and cannot compel China or India to absorb high economic costs on Iran’s behalf." Potentially Tense Armenian Meeting Along with Turkey, other nonmember nations and others participating and observing will include Armenia, Azerbaijan, UN chief Antonio Guterres, and heads of several Moscow-oriented international organizations. Putin is scheduled to meet Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinian, whose country has long been an ally of Russia but which has angered Moscow by seeking to move closer to the West. SEE ALSO: Mobilization Migration: Is There An Uptick In Russians Fleeing Amid Fears Of A New Draft? Tensions heightened between the two countries after Armenian police on August 25 arrested former President Robert Kocharian, now leader of the country's second-largest opposition party, amid accusations of corruption-related offenses. Kocharian, 71, served as Armenia's president between 1998 and 2008. He currently leads the Armenia Alliance, which is considered pro-Moscow and finished third in recent parliamentary elections in June. Yerevan has also angered Moscow by expressing its ambition to eventually join the European Union. SEE ALSO: Former Armenian President Arrested On Corruption Charges "We will insist that Armenia cannot aspire for EU membership while hugely benefiting from cooperation within the European Economic Union (EEU)," said Ushakov, referring to the five-member trade bloc that also includes Belarus, Kazakhstan, and Kyrgyzstan. Following the Bishkek event, Putin is scheduled to travel to Vladivostok for the Eastern Economic Forum on Russia's Pacific coast from September 1-4. He is also set to meet with leaders of several other countries there, including the Indonesian president and Mongolian prime minister. https://www.rferl.org/a/us-sanctions-ira.body: Iran US Sanctions All Remaining Iranian Airlines In Sweeping Aviation Crackdown By Alex Raufoglu September 08, 2026 19:38 CET US Sanctions All Remaining Iranian Airlines In Sweeping Aviation Crackdown Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Mahan Air, which has been under US sanctions since 2011, received at least three Boeing 777 aircraft this summer through a route involving the United Arab Emirates and Oman, according to the US Treasury. (file photo) WASHINGTON -- The United States has imposed sanctions on all of Iran's remaining active airlines, sharply escalating pressure on Tehran's aviation sector as part of a broader campaign aimed at cutting the Islamic republic off from international trade and finance. The US Treasury Department on September 8 sanctioned 36 targets, including 27 Iranian airlines, as well as foreign companies and an individual accused of helping Iran's sanctioned aviation networks procure aircraft, aircraft parts, and other technology. The action marks the first time Washington has used a new August 24 determination targeting Iran's aviation sector to sanction the country's remaining airlines. Treasury said the sector is used by the Iranian government to move weapons, personnel, and illicit cargo. "Let this be a warning to anyone doing business with Iran's remaining airlines, all of which we sanctioned today: You are at risk of being cut off from the global financial system," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said. "We will not relent in our campaign to shut down the Iranian regime's financial lifelines, including the aviation sector," State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said in a statement. SEE ALSO: US Launching 'Economic Onslaught' On Iran, Demands Countries Cut 'Lifelines' That Sustain Tehran The sanctions come under President Donald Trump's so-called Operation Economic Outcast, announced by Bessent on August 24 as part of a campaign to sever what Washington describes as the Iranian regime's remaining economic lifelines. Among the airlines designated are Iran Aseman Airlines, Iran Airtour, Kish Airlines, Qeshm Air, Karun Airlines, Sepehran Airlines, Taban Airlines, Varesh Airlines, Zagros Airlines, Chabahar Airlines, Fly Persia, and Saha Airlines, formally known as the Armed Forces Air Transport Service. Other carriers sanctioned include Air Shiraz, Ava Airlines, Fly Kish, Mehr Airways, Raimon Airways, and Soroush Air. There was no immediate public response from Iran to the September 8 measures. Targeting Iran's Aviation Lifelines The Treasury action goes beyond Iranian carriers, targeting a network of foreign companies that Washington says helped sanctioned Mahan Air acquire aircraft and operate international flights. Mahan Air has been under US counterterrorism sanctions since 2011. Washington accuses the carrier of providing logistical support to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC), including by transporting personnel, weapons, and military equipment. The Treasury said Mahan Air received at least three Boeing 777 aircraft this summer through a route involving the United Arab Emirates and Oman. The UAE-based ECT Aviation Support and Turkey-based Sky Phoenix were identified as intermediaries in what Washington described as a scheme to transfer US-origin aircraft to Mahan Air. ECT Aviation Support's owner and chief executive, Egyptian national Mahran Ibrahim Ali Mohamed Mahran, was also sanctioned. SEE ALSO: Crashes, Bankruptcy Litter Iran's Runway For Passenger-Plane Production Other foreign companies targeted include Malaysia-based iCargo, Kazakhstan-based Tour Invest, and Turkish firms MES Cargo and S Sistem Logistics. Treasury said the companies provided general sales, cargo, logistics, or other services to Mahan Air. S Sistem, for example, was accused of coordinating shipments of unmanned aerial vehicle components and industrial equipment destined for Iran. Treasury said iCargo had coordinated shipments of US-origin parts to Iran on Mahan Air's behalf. Kerri Bitsoff, a former senior official at the US Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control, told RFE/RL that the measures could have a broad impact because of the extent to which international aviation relies on US-origin equipment and technology. "Treasury's action today designated every remaining Iranian airline and pulled the authorizations that let foreign carriers fly US-origin aircraft into Iran," Bitsoff said. "Nearly every commercial plane in the world is US-origin or flies on US-controlled engines and avionics, so that reaches almost the entire global fleet," she added. SEE ALSO: For Iranians Seeking A Way Out, Even The English Test Is Becoming A Barrier Bitsoff said direct air links had been among Tehran's remaining channels to the outside world and accused the Iranian government of using them to move "gold and hard currency," IRGC personnel and weapons, as well as aircraft parts and dual-use components. She said the pressure was particularly significant amid what she described as a broader tightening of economic routes around Iran, with maritime routes restricted, European governments backing the pressure campaign, and Persian Gulf countries reducing trade. "These designations force a choice on every fuel supplier, ground handler, and bank that still touches an Iranian airline," Bitsoff said. Pressure On Intermediaries Treasury also suspended three Iran-related aviation authorizations, including permissions concerning overflights and the operation of US-origin or US-controlled commercial aircraft in Iran by non-US airlines. Requests related to aviation safety will be considered on a case-by-case basis, the department said. Brett Erickson, a sanctions expert at Obsidian Risk Advisors, described the move as a major escalation of Washington's pressure campaign. "This is a significant escalation of Operation Economic Outcast," Erickson told RFE/RL. "Washington is pairing a naval blockade with sanctions designed to close off airspace as an alternative economic route and make it harder for Iran to move goods or buffer its economy." SEE ALSO: Oil Hits 4-Month High As Hormuz, Red Sea Risks Mount The Treasury said foreign companies and individuals that facilitate transactions involving sanctioned Iranian airlines could face serious consequences, including secondary sanctions that could restrict their access to the US financial system. US persons are generally prohibited from conducting transactions involving the blocked entities, while foreign financial institutions can face restrictions on their US correspondent or payable-through accounts for certain significant transactions involving sanctioned parties. Alongside the sanctions, the Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, or FinCEN, issued an alert urging financial institutions to watch for Iranian procurement networks seeking aircraft and aircraft parts through front companies and intermediaries in third countries. The department said Iranian airlines have used companies posing as aviation, technology, or logistics businesses in Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and Asia to acquire Western aircraft, components, and dual-use goods while concealing the ultimate Iranian end-user. The new measures extend Washington's campaign from individual airlines and support companies to virtually the entire commercial aviation infrastructure serving Iran, increasing the risks for foreign businesses that continue to provide Tehran with aircraft, parts, cargo services, sales representation, or financial support. https://www.rferl.org/a/shanghai-securit.body: Features 'Shanghai' Grouping At 25: Rifts, Rivalries, And A Show Of Unity By Zamira Eshanova and RFE/RL's Kyrgyz Service August 31, 2026 21:12 CET 'Shanghai' Grouping At 25: Rifts, Rivalries, And A Show Of Unity Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping meet on August 31 on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek. With a summit in Bishkek, the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) is turning 25 at a moment of extraordinary tension that touches directly on many of the increasingly sprawling regional group's members. Iran is at war with the United States, Russia's war on Ukraine continues to rage with no sign of a let-up, China faces mounting US pressure over trade, and nuclear-armed foes India and Pakistan sit together despite deep rivalry, just to name a few. The four Central Asian members -- host country Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, and Tajikistan -- are regional players but also the objects of various nations seeking to increase their sway, including China, Russia, India, and the United States, which is not a member of the SCO. SEE ALSO: Amid Setbacks, Putin Looks To Restore Russia's Standing At Bishkek SCO Summit In an interview with the People's Daily, the newspaper of the Central Committee of China's Communist Party, SCO Secretary-General Nurlan Yermekbaev of Kazakhstan touted the "Shanghai spirit," which he said involves mutual trust, respect, and benefit, among other qualities he asserted make the group appealing to the so-called Global South. But behind these "shared values" are deep differences, with members using the SCO platform to pursue their own, often competing agendas. Each member "has its own distinct position, and the major powers have views that differ from one another," Kyrgyz political analyst Emil Juraev said. China and India "have differing positions on many issues, and there are also areas of dispute between them," Juraev said. "Russia is trying to exert influence on the world and...continues its war without stopping it. In addition, there is Iran. Everyone is waiting to see what Iran will do." Russian President Vladimir Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi shake hands during a meeting on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) in Bishkek on August 31. The 26th annual SCO summit marks 25 years since it was established by China, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan. India, Pakistan, Iran, and Belarus are now members, and along with observer states and dialogue partners it represents nearly half of the world's population and roughly a quarter of the global economy. "Bishkek has become a world capital today," a local paper proclaimed on August 31 as leaders gathered for bilateral meetings on the eve of the formal summit. The September 1 meeting is expected to produce a Bishkek Declaration marking the anniversary along with thematic statements and decisions covering security, the economy, transport, environmental protection, artificial intelligence, and cultural and humanitarian cooperation. Past gatherings have produced no momentous decisions, however, and for members large and small it may be more about show than substance. Despite deep differences within the organization, the SCO gives its members and observers a platform to appear together on the international stage and project the weight of a larger collective, said Reid Standish, a nonresident research fellow at the Central European Institute of Asian Studies and a former RFE/RL correspondent. "It may not have major policy achievements to its name and it can be hamstrung by its internal rivalries, but the SCO still clearly serves a purpose in bringing these leaders together in a forum that isn't dominated by Western powers," he said. "The SCO's leaders clearly attach meaning to this, otherwise they would not be attending." China is the SCO's most influential member, and its economic weight has put Beijing at the center of mounting international pressure over trade. SEE ALSO: What If China Doesn't Play Ball? US Sanctions Campaign Faces Its Biggest Test Ahead of an August 31 meeting of G20 finance ministers and central bank governors halfway around the world in Asheville, North Carolina, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he would encourage members to rethink their trade with China, calling Beijing's roughly $1.2 trillion global trade surplus unsustainable. Last week, Bessent urged countries to cut ties with Iran as part of an effort to " sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone." For Iran, the signal it hopes the SCO summit will send is that it is not alone. "In the confrontation between Iran and America, we should expect stronger statements here, statements about Western influence and pressure or a declaration expressing disagreement with the processes in Iran or saying something along the lines of, 'You are doing the wrong thing,'" Kyrgyz political analyst Chynara Esengul said. Likewise Russia, which is under increasingly tight Western sanctions over its war against Ukraine. In 2023, the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Putin on suspicion of war crimes over the illegal transfer of Ukrainian children to Russia. For China, Standish said, SCO meetings "serve a useful purpose in providing important optics to the world that key global decisions can be reached without the presence of Western leaders." https://www.rferl.org/a/armenia-tripp-tr.body: Armenia Armenia Courts Central Asia As TRIPP Corridor Takes Shape By Zamira Eshanova and RFE/RL's Kyrgyz Service September 06, 2026 13:34 CET Armenia Courts Central Asia As TRIPP Corridor Takes Shape Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinian speaks at an SCO summit in the Kyrgyz capital, Bishkek, on September 1. Armenia is courting Central Asia as it intensifies efforts to break ground on an ambitious trade corridor named after US President Donald Trump -- the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity, or TRIPP. Part of a peace deal between Yerevan and Baku, the planned corridor would run across Armenian territory, linking Azerbaijan to its Nakhchivan exclave while opening a new east-west trade artery bypassing Russia and Iran. The proposed plan has the backing of Washington, but has riled Moscow and Tehran, two countries under heavy Western sanctions. Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinian has in recent weeks pushed for the involvement of Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan. But both countries, observers say, are wary of angering Russia, a key political and economic player in Central Asia. Pashinian discussed TRIPP with the leaders of Azerbaijan and India as well representatives from the United States during the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Bishkek on September 1. SEE ALSO: Bypassing The Kremlin: Armenia And Azerbaijan Expand Trade, Testing Russia's Grip On August 27, Pashinian confirmed to RFE/RL’s Armenian Service that he had discussed Kazakhstan’s possible participation in TRIPP during a recent phone call with Kazkah President Qasym-Zhomart Tokaev. “We discussed this issue in relation to Kazakhstan and the TRIPP project. Various countries are now showing interest,” Pashinian said, without elaborating. Kyrgyz official Daniyar Amangeldiev told RFE/RL’s Kyrgyz Service that the government had yet to receive an official proposal. Public Rollout While the participation of potential regional partners remains uncertain, Armenia and the United States are moving ahead with plans to publicly launch the project. On September 1, they launched the official TRIPP Armenia Facebook page , jointly managed by the Armenian Foreign Ministry and US Embassy in Yerevan. On the same day, US and Armenian officials met in Armenia’s province of Syunik, where the 43-kilometer-long corridor is planned, to discuss the project and its potential economic benefits. Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinian (left) meets with US President Donald Trump in Egypt in late 2025. The United States owns 74 percent of the project, with Armenia retaining the rest. Washington has committed an initial $145 million. Pashinian has called TRIPP a “multibillion-dollar project.” TRIPP was approved by the Armenian government in July. The Constitutional Court is expected to rule on it on September 15 before it goes to parliament for a final vote. Washington has pledged to help secure additional financing from public and private investors, although no new investors or funds have been announced. For landlocked Armenia, the project is seen as a way to end its economic isolation and become a regional transport hub. SEE ALSO: Armenia Wants In On Asia-Europe Trade. Russian Rail Control Stands In The Way. Unveiled as part of the US-mediated peace process following Armenia's war with Azerbaijan over its breakaway region of Nagorno-Karabakh, TRIPP envisages rail and road infrastructure, possible oil and gas pipelines, and fiber-optic and electricity ventures. Since Azerbaijan regained control over Karabakh in a lightening offensive in September 2023, Armenia has shifted its geopolitical orientation, distancing itself from longtime ally Moscow and aligning more closely with the West. Bishkek, Astana 'Curiously Muted' Kazakhstan has publicly expressed interest in participating in TRIPP. TRIPP would complement the Middle Corridor, an emerging 6,500-kilometer-long trade route, bypassing Russia, that connects China to Europe through Central Asia and the Caucasus. TRIPP would provide onward connectivity from Azerbaijan through Armenia and Nakhchivan to Turkey and Europe. Kyrgyz officials have also presented TRIPP as a potential extension of the country’s transport links to Europe. “Our railway would reach Baku, which would also open a direct route for us to Turkey... It is a new opportunity,” Kyrgyzstan’s ambassador to the United States, Edil Baisalov, told RFE/RL’s Kyrgyz Service. Still, neither Bishkek nor Astana has publicly committed to participating in TRIPP. Kyrgyz political analyst Emilbek Dzhuraev said both countries have been “curiously muted.” SEE ALSO: Russia Uses Economic Chokehold To Counter Armenia's Westward Tilt “While both of them have had positive exchanges with the US, their SCO partners -- Iran in particular, but also Russia -- do not welcome TRIPP, and therefore, probably, they are hesitant at jumping on this opportunity,” Dzhuraev said. Russia, he added, may be the biggest factor behind their caution, given Moscow’s increasingly tense relations with Pashinian’s government. “Russia has a still greater stake in this -- given its collapsing hold on Armenia -- and hence, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan would not be cheered on by Russia to join TRIPP,” he said. https://www.rferl.org/a/kazakhstan-elect.body: News Election Observers Say Kazakh President's Party Had 'Undue Advantage' As It Grabs 70 Percent Of Vote By Zamira Eshanova August 24, 2026 17:36 CET Election Observers Say Kazakh President's Party Had 'Undue Advantage' As It Grabs 70 Percent Of Vote Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Members of a local electoral commission count ballots at a polling station during parliamentary elections in Almaty, southeastern Kazakhstan, on August 23. Four months ago, the Adilet party did not exist. Today, it dominates Kazakhstan’s political landscape, following an election in which it gained 71.17 percent of the vote according to results announced on August 24. The vote marks a further tightening of President Qasym-Zhomart Toqaev's grip on power -- and was roundly criticized by international election observers from the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE). “The 23 August early parliamentary elections, while technically well prepared, took place in an environment lacking political pluralism. Political choice was reduced by the lack of distinct political alternatives, with all contesting parties supporting the incumbent President’s policies,” an OSCE statement said. In the August 24 statement , issued a day after the vote itself, the OSCE reported misuse of public resources, including public-sector employees being mobilized to attend campaign events, and concluded that Adilet had "an undue advantage that blurred the line between state and party.” The OSCE noted that independent candidates had been excluded from the election, a factor which “limited political participation and electoral competitiveness.” Observers also cast doubt on the results themselves, stating that discrepancies between what they saw at polling stations and official turnout data “raised questions about the integrity of the voter turnout reporting and the counting process.” OSCE missions have made similar criticisms of all previous elections held in Kazakhstan since it became independent after the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991, noting a lack of genuine political competition in an authoritarian country dominated for decades by presidents Nursultan Nazarbaev (1991-2019) and his successor, Toqaev. SEE ALSO: Kazakh Voters Appear To Approve Controversial Changes That Critics Say May Concentrate President's Power When Adilet was formed, in April, it absorbed the ruling party that had dominated Kazakhstan during and since the Nazarbaev era. Its stated aim is to implement Toqaev's policies and it will now comfortably control Kazakhstan's new unicameral parliament, the Kurultai. Adilet’s vote share was more than eleven times that of its nearest rival. The election was the first since constitutional changes rammed through by Toqaev earlier this year to switch from a previous bicameral structure. Media Pressure Before the Vote The election took place amid reports of pressure on independent activists and media. Almaty-based civil activist Asset Abishev said police blocked access to his home on August 23, which he described as interference with his right to vote. Another activist, Nurbol Arterkhan, who is under probation and subject to electronic monitoring, said he was repeatedly required to report to probation officials on election day and that police later visited his home. SEE ALSO: Criminal Cases, Travel Bans: Pressure Mounts On Kazakh Journalists Ahead Of Parliamentary Vote According to the Committee to Protect Journalists, five prominent journalists have been jailed or convicted since mid-July, while criminal cases have been opened against two others. Several have also been barred from practicing journalism. Media freedom was another major concern in the OSCE assessment. “Long-standing concerns about arrests and pressure on independent journalists generate pervasive self-censorship,” it noted in its statement. Sevilay Celenk, who headed a team of observers from the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE), also raised the issue. “Without an inclusive, credible, and pluralistic media environment, political participation and representation are fundamentally limited, especially during elections,” Celenk said. New posts 14:24 Houthis Reach Strategic Island On Key Red Sea Shipping Route Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi rebels have reached the strategic island of Perim, also known as Mayyun, in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, potentially strengthening their grip on one of the world's most important shipping routes, according to Yemeni government sources. Iranian President Masud Pezeshkian arrived in the Indian capital, New Delhi, on September 11 to join the leaders of BRICS countries for a summit, with the escalating Middle East conflict expected to feature prominently on the agenda. BRICS, a grouping of major emerging markets and developing countries, takes its name from Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa. It expanded from five to 11 members in 2024 and 2025, adding Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The two-day BRICS Leaders' Summit begins on September 12 and is expected to bring together Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, among other leaders. Iran, which joined BRICS in 2024, is directly involved in the conflict, while fellow member the UAE has faced Iranian missile attacks and taken measures against Tehran. The UAE suspended all trade and financial transactions with Iran in August following the attacks, underscoring growing tensions within BRICS as the summit convenes amid the deepening regional crisis. The UAE is expected to be represented by Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan. https://www.rferl.org/a/iran-infiltratio.body: Iran 'Infiltration' Bill Exposes Iran's Internal Divisions Over Wartime Security Crackdown By Kian Sharifi September 10, 2026 15:43 CET 'Infiltration' Bill Exposes Iran's Internal Divisions Over Wartime Security Crackdown Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf speaks during an event marking 40 days since the burial of Iran's late Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, in Karbala, Iraq, on August 20. Iran's parliament is trying to turn fears of foreign infiltration into law. But as lawmakers work through the legislation, the debate is exposing an increasingly awkward question for the Islamic republic: How far should the state go in policing Iranians' contact with the outside world? At the center of that debate is Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, who, at least publicly, is doing a balancing act. He has defended the need for tougher measures against foreign infiltration while warning that the current draft of the legislation goes too far. "No patriot opposes countering foreign infiltration," Qalibaf said during a recent parliamentary session. But, he added, lawmakers needed to ensure that people's "rights, their lives, and their trade" were not affected. SEE ALSO: Iran Parliament Advances Bill Criminalizing Contact With Foreign Media and Institutions He said security agencies may need to be able to vet Iranians' contacts with foreigners but that they cannot demand permission at every stage. "They say they want to be certain, to have permission sought from them at every stage," the conservative speaker said. "That's not possible, because then we'd have to lock the country down." That balancing act gets to the heart of a bill that was conceived as a wartime response to genuine security failures. The two recent wars exposed how deeply Israeli intelligence had penetrated Iran and prompted calls for tougher measures to identify and prevent foreign influence. But what began as a security response has evolved into a much broader fight over the boundaries of the Islamic republic's security state. The bill, formally called the Plan To Counter The Infiltration Of Intelligence Services And Foreign Governments Or Institutions but commonly referred to as the "infiltration bill," would require Iranians to obtain prior approval from the Intelligence Ministry and the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) Intelligence Organization before engaging in a sweeping range of activities. Those activities include publishing books or articles, academic cooperation, interviews with foreign media deemed "hostile," and participation in scientific conferences or arts festivals. The bill also includes provisions criminalizing interviews, discussions, and other communication with media deemed hostile, as well as sending photographs, videos, audio, or other material to foreign media, with violations punishable by prison terms of up to two years. Parliament approved the bill's general framework in mid-August by a lopsided 183-4 vote. The draft has since expanded from 19 to 33 articles as it has moved through the National Security and Foreign Policy Committee. Only its first two articles have so far cleared the floor, while the remaining provisions remain subject to revision. Even if parliament approves them, the bill will still require Guardian Council approval before it can become law. The political resistance, however, has already begun. SEE ALSO: Oil Hits 4-Month High As Hormuz, Red Sea Risks Mount Qalibaf has sent two of the bill's most consequential provisions -- Articles 7 and 8, which deal with the disclosure process and penalties for exceeding the scope of a permit -- back to the committee because of ambiguities. Qalibaf has insisted that parliament must address the security agencies' concerns, saying their "needs" would be met "within reasonable bounds." But he has rejected the idea that the Intelligence Ministry and IRGC Intelligence Organization should effectively have the power to approve Iranians' foreign contacts at every turn. He has also dismissed suggestions that the bill should be shelved at the government's request. When First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref claimed Qalibaf had privately promised to stop the legislation, an MP repeated the allegation on the parliamentary floor. Qalibaf rejected it, stressing that parliament is not "a branch of the government." The result is a political fault line that does not fit neatly into Iran's usual hardliner-versus-reformist divide. Some lawmakers have been far more openly hostile to the bill. Mohammad Mehdi Shahriari, a member of the National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, called it "completely at odds with national interests." The government of President Masud Pezeshkian has also publicly opposed the bill. Hossein Afshin, the vice president for science, technology, and the knowledge-based economy, warned the current draft could isolate Iran's academic and research community and lead to "scientific stagnation." He pointed to the risks of an accelerated brain drain and additional obstacles for Iranian scientists working or studying abroad. Conservative commentator Mohammad Mohajeri, editor of Khabar Online, made much the same point more sarcastically, writing on X that just as the government was trying to persuade Iranians living abroad to return home, parliament was giving elites, scholars, and students fresh reasons to leave. The controversy has also attracted international criticism. On September 3, the UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran called for the bill to be withdrawn, warning it could further restrict fundamental freedoms and isolate Iranians from the international community. UN Special Rapporteur on Iran Mai Sato separately warned that Iranian intelligence agencies should not become "the gatekeepers of Iranian people's contact with the world." For Iran's political establishment, however, the more immediate problem may be closer to home. Few in the system appear willing to dispute that foreign infiltration is a genuine security threat. The argument is increasingly over what should follow from that threat and where the state should draw the line.
